blocks.text: MCP servers are generous by nature. They exist to hand data over to a client, a file here, a database row there, a config value somewhere else.
That generosity is exactly what makes resources a security surface. Every uri a server is willing to answer is a small promise about what it will and will not show.
This lesson looks at how that promise can break, by accident more often than by attack, and what a careful server author does about it.
1. Resources Are a Security Surface

blocks.alt: A client requests a resource, the server resolves and checks it, then rejects or serves it

blocks.text: A tool call feels dangerous because it can take action. A resource read feels harmless because it only returns data.
That feeling is misleading. Reading the wrong data can be just as damaging as running the wrong action, sometimes worse, because leaks are quiet.
Every resource a server exposes is a door. The question worth asking for each one is simple, who is this door for, and who might walk through it by mistake.
2. What Can Go Wrong When You Expose Resources
Most resource security problems are not clever attacks. They are ordinary oversights that nobody noticed until it was too late.

items: A server meant to expose one report folder accidentally exposes the whole disk because the root was set too broadly.
A resource template built for convenience lets a client substitute any filename, including files nobody meant to share.
A resource description mentions internal system details that should never have left the server.
Error messages returned from a failed resource read reveal folder structure or file existence that helps an attacker map the system.
A resource meant for one user is readable by any authenticated client because nobody added a per user check.

blocks.text: None of these require a sophisticated attacker. They just require a server that trusted itself a little too much.
3. Path Traversal, The Classic Attack

blocks.alt: A malicious URI with dot dot slash tries to escape the intended sandbox

blocks.text: Path traversal is the oldest trick in the book, and it still works because it is so easy to get wrong.
The idea is simple, a client sends a path like dot dot slash dot dot slash etc slash passwd instead of a normal filename.
If the server naively joins that string onto its resource root, the dot dot segments walk the path right back out of the folder it was supposed to stay in.

code.content:
import os

RESOURCE_ROOT = "/data/reports"

def read_resource(uri_path):
    # uri_path comes straight from the client, for example "../../etc/passwd"
    full_path = os.path.join(RESOURCE_ROOT, uri_path)
    with open(full_path, "r") as f:
        return f.read()

blocks.text: This function looks completely reasonable at a glance, and that is the whole problem with path traversal bugs.
4. Why URI to Filesystem Mapping Is Risky
Many MCP servers map a resource uri almost directly onto a filesystem path, because it is the fastest way to build something that works.
That shortcut quietly hands the client partial control over which file gets opened, which is a much bigger grant of trust than it looks like.
The uri is client supplied input, and client supplied input should never be trusted to decide, on its own, which file the server touches.

blocks.title: Treat every uri as hostile
blocks.content: Even a client you built yourself might have a bug that sends a bad uri. Validate as if the input is adversarial, not just as if it might be malformed.

blocks.text: 5. Validating Resource Paths

blocks.alt: A path that passes validation is allowed while one that fails is rejected

blocks.text: Validation means checking the path before it is used, not after, and rejecting anything that looks even slightly off.
A short checklist catches most real problems without needing anything fancy.

items: Reject any raw path containing dot dot segments outright, before doing any resolution.
Resolve the path to its fully expanded, absolute, symlink free form.
Compare that resolved form against the allowed root, not the original unresolved string.
Reject anything that is a symlink pointing outside the allowed root.
Normalize encoding tricks too, a url encoded dot dot is still a dot dot.

blocks.text: The order matters here, resolve first, then compare, because comparing an unresolved string is exactly how traversal bugs slip through.
6. Sandboxing, Building a Real Boundary

blocks.alt: A sandbox boundary confines every resource access inside it

blocks.text: Validation catches obviously bad input. Sandboxing is the deeper habit of never trusting validation alone to hold the line.
A real sandbox means the server physically cannot read outside its allowed root, even if a validation check somewhere gets skipped.
That usually means resolving the real, absolute path first, and only then checking a strict prefix match against the sandbox root.
Notice the sandbox check happens on the resolved candidate, after symlinks and dot dot segments have already been flattened out.
7. Watching One Request Move Through The Checks
It helps to trace a single hostile request end to end, step by step, to see exactly where it gets stopped.
Picture a client asking for a file it should never see, hidden behind a path that looks almost normal.
Notice that the server never opens a file handle until after the resolved path has already passed the boundary check.
That ordering is not an accident, checking after opening the file is too late, the damage is already done by then.
8. Access Control Per Resource

blocks.alt: Each resource carries its own access control check

blocks.text: Staying inside the sandbox root only proves a path is safe from traversal. It says nothing about whether this particular client should see this particular resource.
Those are two separate questions, and a server needs an answer for both, every single time.

blocks.text: The right check depends entirely on what the resource is, which is exactly why per resource rules beat one blanket rule for everything.
9. Avoiding Leaks Through Resource Descriptions
A resource description is metadata, the text a client sees before it even reads the content, and it is easy to forget it counts as exposure too.
Descriptions that mention internal hostnames, real file paths, employee names, or system versions hand out information for free.
A client only needs enough description to decide whether to read the resource, nothing more.

blocks.title: Metadata is still data
blocks.content: Before shipping a resource description, read it as if you were an attacker. Would this sentence tell me something useful that the content itself should not have revealed anyway.

blocks.text: 10. Avoiding Leaks Through Resource Content
Even a resource with correct access control can leak if the content itself contains more than the client actually needs.
A common mistake is returning an entire database row when only two fields were ever relevant to the client task.

items: Strip internal identifiers, database keys, and audit fields that have no meaning to the client.
Never echo credentials, tokens, or connection strings back inside resource content, even for debugging.
Redact or omit fields that belong to other users even if they happened to be in the same query result.
Keep error messages generic, do not reveal internal stack traces or file paths when a read fails.

blocks.text: Think of it as a second, quieter kind of least privilege, applied to the shape of the data rather than to who can request it.
11. The Principle of Least Privilege

blocks.alt: Minimum needed access is compared against granting broad access

blocks.text: Least privilege is an old idea from security engineering, give every actor the smallest amount of access that still lets it do its job.
Applied to MCP, the actor is the client, and the access is every resource, every field, every folder the server is willing to hand over.
The test is always the same question, does this client need this exact thing to do the task in front of it, right now.
12. Applying Least Privilege to Resource Exposure
In practice, least privilege means designing resource exposure narrow first, then widening only when a real need shows up.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Exposure choice","The privileged, risky version","The least privilege version"],"rows":[["Root folder for file resources","The whole home directory","One specific reports subfolder, nothing else"],["Fields returned for a user record","The full database row","Only name, plan, and status fields"],["Resource list visible to a client","Every resource on the server","Only resources tied to that client session"],["Config values exposed as a resource","The entire config file, secrets included","A filtered view with secrets removed"]]}

blocks.text: Every row in that table is the same lesson, wearing a different costume, start narrow and only grant more once a real need earns it.
13. Logging and Auditing Resource Access

blocks.alt: Every resource access is logged for later auditing

blocks.text: Prevention is not the whole story, a server should also be able to answer, after the fact, who read what and when.
Good logs make an attempted traversal attack visible immediately, instead of being discovered weeks later.

blocks.title: Log the attempt, not the secret
blocks.content: Record the uri, the client identity, and the outcome of an access check. Never log the actual sensitive content of a resource just to make debugging easier.

blocks.text: An audit trail also helps with a much less dramatic problem, quietly noticing that a resource is being read far more than expected.
14. Worked Example
Let us walk through a small but complete resource handler that combines sandboxing, access control, and safe error handling together.
Notice the two failure branches both raise the same generic message, resource not found, instead of separately saying blocked by sandbox or blocked by owner check.
That is deliberate, a more specific error would tell a probing client whether a file exists at all, which is itself a small leak.
The owner lookup and the sandbox check are two independent gates, and both must pass before a single byte of content is read from disk.
15. Common Mistakes
These are the mistakes that show up again and again in real MCP servers, usually written by people who meant well.

items: Checking the sandbox boundary against the raw, unresolved path instead of the fully resolved real path.
Trusting a resource template parameter to be a safe filename just because the client interface only offers a dropdown.
Returning detailed error messages that reveal whether a file or folder actually exists on disk.
Writing access control once for the whole server instead of thinking about each resource kind separately.
Putting real internal paths, hostnames, or secrets into a resource description meant to help clients pick a resource.
Forgetting that symlinks can point outside the sandbox root even when the visible path looks perfectly contained.

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Take the vulnerable read_resource function from section three and rewrite it yourself before looking back at section six.

items: Add a check that resolves the path and rejects anything outside the resource root.
Add an owner lookup so a resource can only be read by the user id it belongs to.
Make both failure cases raise the exact same generic error message.
Write down one resource your own project exposes today, and decide honestly whether it currently follows least privilege.

blocks.text: If step four is uncomfortable to answer honestly, that discomfort is usually pointing at the resource worth fixing first.
17. Key Takeaway
Resources feel passive, but every uri a server answers is a decision about trust, made once at design time and then replayed on every request.
Resolve paths before checking them, check access per resource, keep descriptions and content lean, and default every exposure choice to the smallest one that still works.
